Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: 
At the instance of the plaintiff in Testamentary Suit No. 02 of 2015, 
this rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party nos. 1-3 to show 
cause as to why the order no. 15 dated 25.07.2018 passed by the learned 
District Judge as well as District Delegate, Magura in the said suit adding 
the opposite-party nos. 1-3 as defendant nos. 3-5 to the suit on allowing 
application filed for addition of party should not be set aside and/or such 
other or further order or orders be passed as to this court may seem fit and 
proper. 
At the time of issuance of the rule, all further proceeding of the said 
Testamentary Suit was stayed for a period of 6(six) months which was 
lastly extended on 03.04.2019 till disposal of the rule. 
The salient facts so figured in the instant revisional application are: 
The present petitioner as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit seeking 
probate and letter of administration over the property described in the 
schedule of the plaint so left by the testators, Sree Rabindra Nath Sharma 
and Sree Shuvash Chandra Sharma. When the suit was being proceeded, 
the present opposite-party nos. 1-3 filed an application for adding them as 
party stating inter alia that, they got the property in R.S. Plot No. 256 as 
of successor of their father, Aftab Ali Munshi and they have been 
enjoying title and possession over the same which is subject matter of the 
property included in the Will. The said application was taken up for 
hearing by the learned District Judge, Magura and vide impugned order 
dated 25.07.2018 allowed the same adding the applicants as defendant 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
nos. 3-5. It is at that stage, the plaintiff filed the instant revision and 
obtained the rule and order of stay. 
 
Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy along with Ms. Anjuman Ara Begum, the 
learned counsels appearing for the petitioner upon taking us to the 
impugned order at the very outset submits that, no reason has been 
assigned while allowing the application for addition of party is a non-
speaking order. 
The learned counsel in this regard has placed his reliance to the 
decision reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 218 and submits that, in a 
testamentary suit seeking probate and letter of administration, there has 
been no scope for a 3rd party to claim any property described in a Will 
until and unless, such claim is made through testators but in the instant 
case, admittedly no such claim has been made by the opposite-party nos. 
1-3 in their application for addition of party and on that very sole ground, 
the learned counsel finally prays for making the rule absolute by setting 
aside the impugned order. 
 
On the contrary, Mr. Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, the learned 
counsel appearing for the opposite-party no. 1 finds it difficult to refute 
the said legal assertion made by the learned counsel for the petitioner 
which has been settled by our Appellate Division in fortifying section 283 
of the Succession Act, 1925 rather submits that, an observation can be 
made by this Hon’ble court so that the opposite-party nos. 1-3 can 
ventilate their grievance by filing appropriate application or instituting a 
suit since they got the said property as of successors. 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
We have considered the submission so placed by the learned 
counsel for the petitioner and that of the opposite-party no. 1. 
On going through the impugned order, we find that, the order has 
been passed by the trial court in a slipshod and cursory manner without 
assigning any reason whatsoever while adding the opposite-party nos. 1-3 
as defendant nos. 3-5. Furthermore, since it has already been settled by 
our Appellate Division reported in 1981 BLD 218 while interpreting 
section 283 of the Succession Act, 1925 that, in a suit for probate and 
letter of administration, no one can made party to contest the suit until and 
unless, they claim the property in the Will through testator. For the ready 
reference let us reproduce the proposition so held by our Appellate 
Division here: 
“Probate proceeding– Addition of party– 
Person not claiming interest in the property through 
the testator not entitled to be added as a party. 
The “interest” in the estate of the testator within the 
words of section 283 means an interest through the 
testator. A person who claims outside or independently 
of the Will (sic) (Estate) of claims adversely to the 
testator and disputes his right to deal with the property 
cannot be deemed to claim any interest in the estate of 
the deceased. The crucial point in this case is whether 
the respondents claim any interest in the estate 
through the testator, and since they do not and cannot 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
do so, they got no locus standi to be added as a party 
to the probate proceeding.” 
  In the instant case, an application for addition of party has been 
filed claiming that they got the property from their father whose name R.S 
record was prepared. But as per section 283 of the Succession Act, there 
has been no scope to be added as party in a Testamentary Suit claiming 
land as co-sharer by inheritance or co-sharer by purchase other than, 
through the testator. So there has been no scope for the opposite-party 
nos. 1-3 to be added as defendants in a testamentary suit. 
Insofar as regards to the submission placed by the learned counsel 
for the opposite-party no. 1 praying for giving the opposite-party nos. 1-3 
avenue to assert their title but we don’t find any substance in the said 
submission because if they are not entitled to be added any defendant in 
the suit then their position cannot be established in the instant suit which 
we are only adjudicating. 
Be that as it may, it has already been found that, no reason has been 
assigned by the trial court in the impugned order for allowing the 
application vis-à-vis there has been explicit legal bar for the opposite-
party nos. 1-3 to be added as a party in a testamentary suit who admittedly 
did not claim the property through the testator so for that obvious reason, 
the impugned order cannot sustain. 
Resultantly, the rule is made absolute however without any order as 
to cost.   
The impugned judgment and order dated 25.07.2018 passed by the 
learned District Judge, Magura in Testamentary Suit No. 02 of 2015 is 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
thus set aside resulting in, the name of the defendant nos. 3-5 are struck 
down from the plaint. 
The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule stands 
vacated. 
Let a copy of the judgment be communicated to the court 
concerned forthwith. 
 
Md. Bashir Ullah, J: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     I agree.

input_summary: The plaintiff in a testamentary suit of 2015 at Magura sought probate and letters of administration over the property left by two testators, and three strangers to the will then applied to be added as defendants, saying that they had inherited a plot from their father, that the plot was recorded in their names, and that it formed part of the property dealt with by the will. The district delegate entertained their application and added them, and the executor came here in revision with a stay of the testamentary proceedings.
explanation: The court read section 283 of the Succession Act and the decisions on who may be heard in a probate proceeding, and held that a party may be added only if he claims an interest in the estate through the testator, since the question in such a suit is the validity of the will and not the title of strangers. The applicants claimed nothing through the testators but asserted a title of their own derived from their father, so they had no standing in the testamentary suit. The order under challenge also assigned no reasons at all, and the names of the added defendants were therefore struck off the plaint.

input_summary: In 2012 the revenue authorities published a list of vested property that included 375 ajutangsha of land at Matuail under Demra in Dhaka, being part of a plot in the settlement records. The petitioner, who traced his title through a series of transfers beginning with a sale of 1955 by one of the recorded tenants, challenged that inclusion under Article 102, and two later purchasers from him joined, saying they had bought the land by a registered deed of 2017, built a tin shed factory there and let it out, and could not get their names mutated.
explanation: The court traced the chain of title through the successive deeds and found that the land had moved out of the hands of the original recorded tenants long before the property came to be listed, and that nothing in the record supported its characterisation as abandoned property. It observed that the petitioners were in possession and that no step had been taken to disturb them, and that the purchasers had invested their own money in the land. Since there was a clear title, the court held that justice required the land to be taken out of the list, and directed the respondents to release it within six months.

input_summary: A primary school was nationalised in 2013, but the post held by one of its teachers was left out of the reorganisation, so she was not taken over into government service with her colleagues. She made a representation, on which the Director General of Primary Education sent a recommendation to the Secretary of the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education in April 2018 asking that her service be brought into the revenue set up. explanation: The court heard the petitioner's advocate and the deputy attorney general and found that the recommendation had been lying with the ministry since April 2018 without any decision, which left the petitioner in suspense about her service despite the recommendation in her favour. input_summary: The widow of a man described as a freedom fighter complained that the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs had suddenly stopped paying the state honorarium due to her from July 2015, and that her husband's name had never been published in the official gazette as a freedom fighter. The heirs of the deceased applied to the ministry in March 2021 for release of the arrears and for the gazette publication, and received no reply at all, nor any further payment. The widow then applied under Article 102 and obtained a rule calling on the ministry to answer for the failure.
explanation: The court heard the petitioner's advocate and the reply of the deputy attorney general, and observed that the claim had been pending before the ministry for years without any response, which left the widow without the allowance to which she said she was entitled. A direction was accordingly given to decide the application within thirty days.

In the instant appeal, the convict-appellant has challenged the 
legality of the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 
31.03.2019 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd 
Court, Naogaon in Sessions Case No. 1286 of 2018 arising out of 
C.R. Case No. 1250 of 2017 convicting the appellant under section 
138 the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him to 
suffer simple imprisonment for ten months and also to pay fine of 
Tk. 11,15,000/-.  
 
None appears on behalf of the appellant when the matter is 
called on for hearing. 
The learned Advocate appearing for the complainant-
respondent No. 2 submits that the charge brought against the 
convict-appellants under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Act, 1881 (in short, ‘the Act, 1881’) has been proved beyond 
reasonable doubt and therefore, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 
 
I have heard the learned Advocate for the complainant-
respondent No. 2 and perused the materials on record. 
 
It appears from the petition of complaint, the deposition of 
PW1 (complainant) and the documentary evidences that the convict-
appellant issued cheque in question in favour of the complainant-
respondent on 17.09.2017 for repayment of outstanding amount of 
Tk. 11,00,000/- which he took from the complainant. The value of 
the cheque is Tk. 11,00,000/-. It was dishonoured by the bank 
concerned on 20.09.2017. The complainant sent the statutory legal 
notice to the convict-appellant on 28.09.2017 and received the same 
on 15.10.2017. The value of the cheque was not paid to the 
complainant. The case was filed on 19.11.2017. P.W.1 proved the 
prosecution case.  
 
I have no hesitation to hold that the complainant-respondent 
has proved compliance of the procedure laid down in Section 138 of 
the Act, 1881 in filing the case. The case was filed within one 
month of the date on which the cause of action had arisen under 
clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138. The complainant also 
proved consideration against which the cheque was drawn and that 
he is the holder of the cheque in due course. Hence, in my view, the 
impugned judgment and order of conviction does not suffer from 
any illegality or infirmity. The trial Court correctly found the 
appellants guilty of the charge.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
 
Section 138 of the Act, 1881 provides that the offence of 
dishonour of cheque is punishable with imprisonment for a term 
which may extend to 1 (one) year, or with fine which may extend to 
thrice the amount of the cheque, or with both. Sub-section (2) of 
Section 138 provides, “Where any fine is realised under sub-section 
(1), any amount up to the face value of the cheque as far as is 
covered by the fine realised shall be paid to the holder”. Thus, the 
criminal proceeding under Section 138 serves two purposes: firstly, 
to punish the offender and secondly, to recover the value of the 
cheque. The object of adding sub-section (2) to Section 138 is to 
alleviate the grievance of the complainant. In the instant case, the 
value of the dishonoured cheque is Tk. 11,00,000/- whereas the 
convict-appellant was fined Tk. 11,15,000/- which requires 
interference.  
 
Now, I turn to the sentence of imprisonment. There can be no 
dispute in so far as the sentence of imprisonment is concerned that it 
should commensurate with the gravity of the crime. Court has to 
deal with the offenders by imposing proper sentence by taking into 
consideration the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not only 
the rights of the offenders which are required to be looked into at 
the time of the imposition of sentence, but also of the victims of the 
crime and society at large, also by considering the object sought to 
be achieved by the particular legislation. Considering the facts and 
circumstances of the case and the object of the law, I am of the view 
that the sentence of imprisonment would be a harsh sentence having 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
no penal objective to be achieved. Hence, the sentence of 
imprisonment is set aside. 
 
I note that the trial court has not passed any default order i.e. 
imprisonment in default of payment of the fine. When an offender is 
sentenced to fine only, the Court has the power to make a default 
order under Section 388 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (in short 
the ‘Cr.P.C.’). Section 423(1)(d) of the Cr.P.C. empowers the 
Appellate Court to pass any consequential or incidental order that 
may be ‘just and proper’. Since, this Court has already set aside the 
sentence of imprisonment, it would be just and proper to pass a 
default order. 
 
In view of the foregoing discussions, the order of the Court is 
as follows: 
The conviction of the appellants under Section 138 of the Act, 
1881 is upheld, but the sentence is modified. The sentence of 
10(then) months simple imprisonment is set aside. The sentence of 
fine of Tk. 11,15,000/- is modified to Tk. 11,00,000/- which is 
equivalent to the value of the dishonoured cheque. The convict-
appellant has already deposited Tk. 5,50,000/- in the Court below 
before filing the appeal. The Court concerned is directed to give the 
said deposit to the complainant-respondent No.2 forthwith. The 
convict-appellant is directed to pay the remaining portion of the 
value of the dishonoured cheque i.e. Tk. 5,50,000/- to the 
complainant-respondent No. 2 within 4(four) months from the date 
of receipt of this order, in default he will suffer simple 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
imprisonment for 01(one) month. If the convict-appellant do not pay 
the remaining portion of the fine as ordered or opts to serve out the 
period of imprisonment in lieu of payment of fine, they are not 
exempted from paying the same. In that event, the Court concerned 
shall realize the fine under the provisions of Section 386 of the 
Cr.P.C. 
 
In the result, the appeal is dismissed with modification of 
sentence and with directions made above. The convict-appellants 
are released from the bail bond. 
Send down the lower Court’s records (LCR) at once. 
Communicate the judgment and order to the Court concerned 
forthwith.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mamnoon Rahman, J:
input_summary: The appellant had been convicted by the additional sessions judge at Naogaon of dishonouring a cheque for Tk. 11,00,000 issued in September 2017 in repayment of a debt of the same amount, the instrument having been returned unpaid three days later, the statutory notice sent on 28 September 2017 having been received on 15 October and no payment having followed, so that the complaint came in November 2017. He was sentenced to ten months' simple imprisonment and a fine of Tk. 11,15,000, and he appealed, but no one appeared to argue his case.
explanation: The court read the complaint, the complainant's deposition and the documentary evidence and found that the statutory sequence had been complied with, that consideration was proved and that the complainant was a holder in due course, so the finding of guilt stood. On the punishment it reasoned that once the fine restores the whole value of the cheque to the holder, a concurrent term of imprisonment achieves nothing, and that as the trial judge had omitted to provide for default, the appellate court could supply one. It therefore undid the custodial sentence, reduced the fine to the value of the cheque and gave four months for the balance.

conviction and sentence dated 05.11.2023 passed by the learned Judge 
(District and Sessions Judge) of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjaton Damon 
Tribunal No. 3, Habiganj in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjaton Damon Case No. 
148 of 2020 arising out of G.R. No. 52 of 2020 corresponding to 
Nabiganj Police Station Case No. 15 dated 23.03.2020, convicting the 
appellant and another accused, namely Dhananjoy Deb under sections 
11(Ga), 30 of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjaton Damon Ain, 2000 (as 
amended 2003) and sentencing them to suffer rigorous imprisonment 
for three years along with a fine of Tk. 50,000/- in default to suffer 
simple imprisonment for another one year more. 
Present 
   Mr. Justice Mamnoon Rahman 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The prosecution case in short, is that, one Sanchita Dhar being 
informant lodged a First Information Report on 23.03.2020 with 
Nabiganj Police Station against five accused persons under sections 
11(Ga), 30 of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjaton Damon Ain, 2000 (as 
amended 2003) alleging inter-alia that the victim is the daughter of the 
informant who was married with the accused No. 1 on 14.11.2018. The 
accused No. 1 staying in Australia and he demanded a dowry of Tk. 
10,00,000/-. Subsequently, the accused persons tortured the victim on 
different occasions and ultimately on the date of occurrence all the 
accused persons indiscriminately injured the victim. Also the accused 
Nos. 1 and 2 injured the victim with stick, the informant rescued the 
victim and took her to the hospital for medical treatment and they tried 
to settle the matter amicably and as they failed to do so the informant 
filed the case. 
The police registered the case as Nabiganj Police Station Case 
No. 15 against the accused persons and proceeded the investigation. 
The Investigation Officer submitted charge sheet being No. 94 dated 
4.7.2020 impleading five accused persons. The trial court discharged 
three accused persons and proceeded against the appellant as well as 
another accused person. During trial the prosecution adduced as many 
as nine witnesses and defence adduced none. The trial court thereafter 
exhausting all the procedures vide the impugned judgment and order 
convicted and sentenced the appellant and another. Being aggrieved the 
present appellant moved before this court by way of appeal. 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
  Mr. Ujjal Paul, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the 
appellant submits that the court below without applying its judicial 
mind and without considering the facts and circumstances most 
illegally and in an arbitrary manner passed the impugned judgment and 
order of conviction and sentence which requires interference by this 
court. He submits that in the present case in hand the court below failed 
to appreciate the legal position as much as failed to notice the 
contradiction in between the testimony of the witnesses and other 
extenuating circumstances and as such the impugned judgment and 
order of conviction and sentence is liable to be set aside for ends of 
justice. The learned counsel placed the evidences and submits that 
though the witnesses corroborated about the time, place and manner 
and occurrence but they are highly interested witnesses as much as by 
referring the deposition of P.Ws. 3 and 4 he submits that though both 
the witnesses are independent but they are very closed to the father of 
the victim and as much as the prosecution failed to produce two vital 
witnesses as cited by P.W. 4 in his deposition. He also submits that the 
doctor who proved the medical report did not examine the victim in 
person which also creates a serious doubt in the prosecution case.      
Ms. Taifoor Kabir, the learned Deputy Attorney General 
appearing on behalf of the opposite party/state vehemently opposes the 
Appeal. He submits that the court below on proper appreciation of the 
facts and circumstances, evidence both oral and documentary as well as 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
the relevant provisions of law passed the impugned judgment and order 
of conviction and sentence which requires no interference by this court. 
I have perused the impugned judgment and order passed by the 
lower appellate court as well as trial court. I have perused the 
memorandum of appeal, grounds taken thereon, necessary papers and 
documents as well as the LC records and I have heard the learned 
Advocate for the petitioners as well as the learned Deputy Attorney 
General for the State. 
On perusal of the same, it transpires that the appellant along with 
another stood charge before the trial court for an offence committed 
under sections 11(Ga), 30 of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjaton Damon Ain, 
2000. The mother of the victim Sanchita Dhar being informant lodged a 
First Information Report resulting which the police initiated a regular 
case and investigated the same. It transpires that after investigation the 
police submitted charge sheet and implicated five accused persons. 
Eventually, the trial court discharged three others and proceeded 
against the appellant and another. The allegation as it transpires from 
the trend of the examination and cross-examination is that the victim 
was married to Dhananjoy Deb who resides in Australia. After 
marriage the accused persons claiming dowry on different occasions 
and ultimately on the date of occurrence they demanded dowry and 
further stated that they will not allow the victim to enter into the house 
as they approached the house all the accused persons indiscriminately 
attacked the victim and the informant and the accused Nos. 1 and 2 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
caused different injuries and the body of the victim. Thereafter, the 
informant rescued the victim and took her hospital for medical 
treatment. 
Informant deposed before the court as P.W. 1 and supported the 
version stated in the First Information Report. P.W. 2 is the husband of 
the informant who stated that he went to the place of occurrence after 
hearing about the occurrence from his wife. P.W. 3 is a local witness. 
In his deposition he stated that he went to the place of occurrence and 
found the door was locked, however, somehow he managed to see that 
the accused persons are torturing the victim. In his cross-examination 
he stated that he well known to the P.W. 2. P.W. 4 is also a local 
witness. In his deposition he stated that after hearing call from the P.W. 
2 and went to the place of occurrence. In his cross-examination he 
stated that the accused persons demanded dowry in presence of 
Upazilla Chairman namely Selim Chowdhury and another Syfuzzaman 
Chowdhury. P.W. 5 is the mother of the victim who in her deposition 
corroborated the deposition made by the informant as P.W. 1. P.W. 6 is 
the relation who heard the occurrence from the informant. P.W. 7 is the 
brother of the victim who is also a hearsay witness. P.W. 8 is the doctor 
who took the medical report but in his cross-examination stated that he 
did not examine the victim and P.W. 9 is the Investigation Officer. 
So, on meticulous perusal of the deposition of the witnesses, it 
transpires that P.W. 9 is the Investigation Officer and P.W. 8 is the 
medical doctor. On further meticulous perusal of the evidence of P .W. 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
8 it transpires that the doctor certified the medical report but he did not 
examine the victim in person though he was the member of the Board. 
Apart from these P.Ws. all are relation of the victim except P.Ws. 3 and 
4. On perusal of the cross-examination of P.Ws. 3 and 4 it transpires 
that they are well known to the father of the victim and they went to the 
place of occurrence after receiving the call from P.W. 2 the husband of 
the informant. It further transpires that as per the depositions of P.Ws. 3 
and 4 they went to the place of occurrence but they cannot enter into 
the house but they somehow managed to see the occurrence. 
So, on meticulous perusal of the papers and documents, it further 
transpires that there is a serious contradiction regarding the manner, 
place, time and occurrence. On perusal of the depositions of the P.Ws, 
it transpires that except P.Ws. 1 and 5 they are no exact eye witness of 
the occurrence in question. P.Ws. 3 and 4 in their depositions stated 
that they got information and called from P.W. 2 about daughter and 
they went to the place of occurrence but they did not mention about the 
distance or how they reached in the place of occurrence. It further 
transpires from their depositions that they somehow managed to see 
from outside of the house that the accused person including the 
appellant is causing injury in the body of the victim.  
Apart from that it also transpires that there is a delay in filing of 
the First Information Report which was not properly explained. So; it 
transpires that in the present case in hand the prosecution failed to 
prove the charge against the present appellant beyond all reasonable 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
doubt though in the First Information Report and from the deposition of 
P.W. 1 it transpires that all the accused persons started beating the 
victim. 
Considering the facts and circumstances, I find substance in the 
instant appeal which is required to be allowed. Accordingly, the instant 
appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order of conviction and 
sentence passed by the court below so far it relates to the present 
appellant is hereby set aside and the appellant be discharged from the 
bail bond.

Both were sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment with a fine. In appeal the appellant attacked the evidence of the witnesses and the delay in setting the law in motion.
explanation: The court went through the depositions and found that apart from the informant and one other, none of the witnesses had seen the occurrence, the two neighbours having reached the house only after being called and having admittedly been unable to enter it, though they claimed to have seen the beating from outside. It found serious contradictions about the manner, the place and the time of the occurrence, and that the medical report had been certified by a doctor who never examined the girl in person though he sat on the board. The delay in the first information report had gone unexplained, and the charge was not established beyond doubt.

Mr. Md. Lokman Hossain, AAG 
Mr. Md. Hatem Ali, AAG 
…… For the Respondent No. 2 
 
 
 
 
 
Heard & Judgment on: 01.08.2024 
 
In the instant appeal, the convict-appellant has challenged the 
legality of the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 
21.03.2019 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd 
Court, Kishoregonj convicting the appellant under section 138 of the 
Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 and sentencing him to suffer 
imprisonment for 6 (six) months and to pay a fine of Tk. 2,05,000/- 
(two lac five thousand) in Sessions Case No. 479 of 2018 arising out 
of C.R. Case No. 21(1)18 which is equivalent to the value of the 
dishonoured cheque.  
 
Mr. A.K.M. Shamsad, the learned Advocate appearing for the 
convict-appellant, submits that the appellant is in no way involved 
in the alleged offence and he has falsely been implicated in this case 
and the impugned judgment and order of conviction has been passed 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
only on the basis of P.W-1 of the complainant-respondent No. 2 and 
not by any independent/neutral witness and as such the same is 
liable to be set aside for the ends of justice. 
The learned Advocate appearing for the complainant-
respondent No. 2 submits that the charge brought against the 
convict-appellants under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments 
Act, 1881 (in short, ‘the Act, 1881’) has been proved beyond 
reasonable doubt and therefore, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 
 
I have heard the learned Advocates for the convict-appellant 
as well as complainant-respondent No. 2 and perused the materials 
on record. 
 
It appears from the petition of complaint, the deposition of 
PW1 (complainant) and the documentary evidences that the convict-
appellant issued cheque in question in favour of the complainant-
respondent on 21.11.2017 for repayment of outstanding amount of 
Tk. 2,00,000/- which he took from the complainant. The value of 
the cheque is Tk. 2,00,000/-. It was dishonoured by the bank 
concerned on 21.11.2017 and subsequently the complainant sent the 
statutory legal notice to the convict-appellant on 28.11.2017. The 
value of the cheque was not paid to the complainant. The case was 
filed on 09.01.2018. P.W.1 proved the prosecution case.  
 
I have no hesitation to hold that the complainant-respondent 
has proved compliance of the procedure laid down in Section 138 of 
the Act, 1881 in filing the case. The case was filed within one 
month of the date on which the cause of action had arisen under 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138. The complainant also 
proved consideration against which the cheque was drawn and that 
he is the holder of the cheque in due course. Hence, in my view, the 
impugned judgment and order of conviction does not suffer from 
any illegality or infirmity. The trial Court correctly found the 
appellants guilty of the charge.  
 
Section 138 of the Act, 1881 provides that the offence of 
dishonour of cheque is punishable with imprisonment for a term 
which may extend to 1 (one) year, or with fine which may extend to 
thrice the amount of the cheque, or with both. Sub-section (2) of 
Section 138 provides, “Where any fine is realised under sub-section 
(1), any amount up to the face value of the cheque as far as is 
covered by the fine realised shall be paid to the holder”. Thus, the 
criminal proceeding under Section 138 serves two purposes: firstly, 
to punish the offender and secondly, to recover the value of the 
cheque. The object of adding sub-section (2) to Section 138 is to 
alleviate the grievance of the complainant. In the instant case, the 
value of the dishonoured cheque is Tk. 2,00,000/- whereas the 
convict-appellant was fined Tk. 2,05,000/- which requires 
interference.  
 
Now, I turn to the sentence of imprisonment. There can be no 
dispute in so far as the sentence of imprisonment is concerned that it 
should commensurate with the gravity of the crime. Court has to 
deal with the offenders by imposing proper sentence by taking into 
consideration the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not only 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
the rights of the offenders which are required to be looked into at 
the time of the imposition of sentence, but also of the victims of the 
crime and society at large, also by considering the object sought to 
be achieved by the particular legislation. Considering the facts and 
circumstances of the case and the object of the law, I am of the view 
that the sentence of imprisonment would be a harsh sentence having 
no penal objective to be achieved. Hence, the sentence of 
imprisonment is set aside. 
 
I note that the trial court has not passed any default order i.e. 
imprisonment in default of payment of the fine. When an offender is 
sentenced to fine only, the Court has the power to make a default 
order under Section 388 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (in short 
the ‘Cr.P.C.’). Section 423(1)(d) of the Cr.P.C. empowers the 
Appellate Court to pass any consequential or incidental order that 
may be ‘just and proper’. Since, this Court has already set aside the 
sentence of imprisonment, it would be just and proper to pass a 
default order. 
 
In view of the foregoing discussions, the order of the Court is 
as follows: 
The conviction of the appellants under Section 138 of the Act, 
1881 is upheld, but the sentence is modified. The sentence of 
06(six) months imprisonment is set aside. The sentence of fine of 
Tk. 2,05,000/- is modified to Tk. 2,00,000/- which is equivalent to 
the value of the dishonoured cheque. The convict-appellant has 
already deposited Tk. 1,00,000/- in the Court below before filing the 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
appeal. The Court concerned is directed to give the said deposit to 
the complainant-respondent No.1 forthwith. The convict-appellant is 
directed to pay the remaining portion of the value of the 
dishonoured cheque i.e. Tk. 1,00,000/- to the complainant-
respondent No. 1 within 4(four) months from the date of receipt of 
this order, in default he will suffer simple imprisonment for 01(one) 
month. If the convict-appellant do not pay the remaining portion of 
the fine as ordered or opts to serve out the period of imprisonment 
in lieu of payment of fine, they are not exempted from paying the 
same. In that event, the Court concerned shall realize the fine under 
the provisions of Section 386 of the Cr.P.C. 
 
In the result, the appeal is dismissed with modification of 
sentence and with directions made above. The convict-appellants 
are released from the bail bond. 
Send down the lower Court’s records (LCR) at once. 
Communicate the judgment and order to the Court concerned 
forthwith.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mamnoon Rahman, J:
input_summary: The appellant had been convicted by the additional sessions judge at Kishoreganj in 2019 of dishonouring a cheque for Tk. 2,00,000 drawn in November 2017 in repayment of money borrowed from the complainant, and sentenced to six months' imprisonment with a fine of Tk. 2,05,000, being the value of the instrument, in a case of 2018. In appeal his advocate argued that he had been implicated falsely and that the finding rested entirely on the complainant's own testimony, with no independent or neutral witness to support it, so that the conviction could not stand.
explanation: The court noted that the only point taken was the absence of an independent witness, and held that the statute does not require the complainant's case to be corroborated, so long as the statutory steps are shown. It found that the complainant had proved the dishonour, the notice and the filing of the complaint within the prescribed month, and that consideration and his status as holder in due course were established, leaving no ground to disturb the conviction. It took the view, however, that a jail term served no purpose where the fine already returned the value of the cheque, and removed it while supplying a default order.

<<PAGE 1>>
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
 
 
 
 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
 
 
        (CIVIL REVISIONAL JURISDICTION) 
 
 
 
Civil  Revision No. 2250 of 2023 
 
 
 
In the matter of: 
An Application under section 115(4) of the Code of 
Civil Procedure, 1908 
 
And 
In the matter of: 
 
Mahmudul Islam Chowdhury  
and others 
 
 
…Petitioners. 
 
 
 
 
 
-Vs- 
East West Container Terminals Limited 
 and others. 
 
 
…Opposite parties. 
 
 
 
 
Mr. A.F. Hassan Arif, Sr. Adv. with 
Mr. T.M. Shakil Hasan, Adv.   
 
 
    
 
 
 
  
 
 …For the petitioners. 
 
 
 
Mr. Fida M. Kamal, Sr. Adv. with 
 
 
 
Mr. Md. Monzur Rabbi, Adv. 
 
 
 
 
...For the opposite parties. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Heard on: 13.05.2024 
And 
Judgment on: The 21st May, 2024 
 
In an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908 rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to 
show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 
02.12.2021 passed by the learned District Judge, Chattogram in Civil 
Revision No. 168 of 2021 rejecting the revision and affirming thereby 
judgment and order No. 11 dated 10.10.2021 passed by the learned Joint 
District Judge, 2nd Court, Chattogram in Other Suit No. 367 of 2020 
rejecting the petition of the defendant Nos. 1-11 dated 08.03.2021 filed 
under Order 7, Rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further 
order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.  
   Present  
          Mr. Justice Mamnoon Rahman 
 
 
 
 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The short facts relevant for the disposal of this rule, are that, the 
opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 367 of 2020 in 
the court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chattogram impleading the 
opposite party as defendants for the following reliefs; 
a) A decree be passed for cancellation of the registered Deed of 
Irrevocable General Power of Attorney, bearing Deed No. 552 
dated 25.01.2017 as shown in 'Schedule A' and registered in 
the Office of Sub-Registrar, Sitakunda, Chattogram in respect 
of the Companies shown in 'Schedule B', 'Schedule C' and 
'Schedule D', 
b) A decree be passed declaring M.A Bakar, Mesbah Uddin and 
Abul Hashem to be the Directors of the Saleh Carpet Mills 
Limited [as shown in 'Schedule B']. Saleh Jute Industries 
Limited [as shown in 'Schedule C'] and Saleh Zarina Limited 
[as shown in 'Schedule D']. 
c) A decree and order be passed directing the defendant No. 12 
Sub-Registrar, Sitakunda, Chattogram, Bangladesh to insert 
necessary information, note and explanation on the concerned 
page[s] of the respective registrar or balam book as to the 
cancellation of the Deed of Irrevocable General Power of 
Attorney, Deed No. 552 dated 25.01.2017. 
d) That the cost of the suit be declared in favour of the plaintiff 
against the contesting defendants, and/or 
e) That the plaintiff be given such other relief or reliefs as may be 
found entitled according to law and equity and such other or 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
further order or orders may be passed as your Honour may 
deem fit and proper. 
The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that, the plaintiff is a private 
limited company duly incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and 
the defendant No. 1 is the holder of the impugned Irrevocable General 
Power of Attorney bearing Deed No. 552 dated 25.01.2017. The 
defendants Nos. 2-11 are the executants of the impugned Irrevocable 
General Power of Attorney bearing Deed No. 552 dated 25.01.2017. The 
defendants Nos. 12-14 are proforma-defendants; that the plaintiff East 
West Container Terminals Limited [East West] purchased the entire 
shares of Saleh Carpet Mills Limited [Saleh Carpet], Saleh Jute 
Industries Limited [Saleh Jute] and Saleh Sarina Limited [Saleh Zarina] 
through 03 [three] Deeds of Agreement dated 28.08.2008 executed 
between the erstwhile share-holders of Saleh Carpet Mills Limited, 
Saleh Jute Industries Limited and Saleh Zarina Limited and East, West 
Container Terminals Limited represented by its Managing Director, that 
as stipulated in the Deed of Agreements dated 28.06.2008 within 01 
(one) year from the date of signing the Deed of Agreements, East West 
Container Terminals Limited paid BDT. 5.00 crore for Saleh Carpet 
Mills Limited, BDT. 2.00 crore for Saleh Jute Limited, BDT> 1.00 crore 
for Saleh Zarina Limited, totaling to BDT. 8.00 crore to the former share 
holders of these companies as a share purchase consideration and that on 
20.09.2011, East West Container Terminals Limited submitted 
applications to Sonali Bank Limited regarding waiver of interest for 
payment of dues of Saleh Carpet Mills Limited, Saleh Jute Industries 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
Limited and Saleh Zarina Limited. On 20.09.2011 the former 
management of Saleh Carpet Mills Limited sent a letter to Sonali Bank 
Limited in support of the waiver of interest application by East West 
Container Terminals Limited and on 23.11.2011 Sonali Bank Limited 
sent letters to East West Container Terminals Limited notifying approval 
of waiver of interest and after the waiver of interest, the total outstanding 
liability of East West Container Terminals Limited regarding Saleh 
Carpet Mills Limited, Saleh Jute Industries Limited and Salch Jute 
Industries Limited had become BDT. 52.00 crore, the Deputy General 
Manager of Agrabad Corporate Branch of Sonali Bank Limited, without 
any legitimate authority, sent a letter dated 18 May, 2015 to East West 
Container Terminals Limited stating that the decision of Waiver of 
interest as was approved by the Board of Directors of Sonali Bank 
Limited had become invalid; that East West Container Terminals 
Limited is continuing with its negotiation with Sonali Bank Limited 
regarding the waiver of interest and has sent several applications to 
Sonali Bank Limited dated 12.12.2016, 04.12.2017, 04.07.2018. The 
approach of the former management of Saleh Carpet Mills Limited, 
Saleh Jute Industries Limited and Saleh Jute Industries Limited and the 
illegally appointed attorney in recent times is completely unaccepted and 
unreasonable. On 11.03.2020 and 19.08.2020, the defendant No. 1, 
Mahmudul Islam Chowdhury sent 2 (two) different letters to the Sonali 
Bank Limited claiming himself to be the Managing Director of Saleh 
Carpet Mills Limited, Saleh Jute Industries Limited and Saleh Jute 
Industries Limited; that in view of the above the plaintiff is entitled to 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
get cancelation of the deed of Power of Attorney bearing Deed No. 552 
dated 25.01.2017 and declaration to the effect that the plaintiff has right, 
title and interest in the management of the schedule properties s 
purchaser of shares. 
The petitioner-defendant entered appearance by filing power to 
contest the suit. Subsequently, the petitioners who are the defendants 
pressed an application under Order 7, Rule 11 read with section 151 of 
the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for rejection of plaint on 08.03.2021. 
The trial court proceeded with the said application and ultimately after 
hearing the parties and considering the facts and circumstances, vide 
Order No. 11 dated 10.10.2021 rejected the application for rejection of 
plaint. The petitioner being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the 
aforesaid judgment and order passed by the trial court rejecting the 
application under Order 7, Rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure, 1908 preferred revision before the learned District 
Judge, Chattogram being Civil Revision No. 168 of 2021 and the 
revisional court after hearing the parties and considering the facts and 
circumstances vide order dated 02.12.2021 rejected the revision and 
thereby affirmed the order passed by the trial court. Being aggrieved by 
and dissatisfied with the said order the petitioners moved before this 
court and obtained the present rule.  
The opposite party-plaintiffs contested the rule by filing 
application for discharging the rule by adducing papers and documents.  
Mr. A. F. Hassan Arif, the learned senior counsel appearing on 
behalf of the petitioners, submits that the courts below in the present 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
case in hand without applying their judicial mind and without 
considering the facts and circumstances, provisions of law, most illegally 
and in an arbitrary manner passed the impugned judgment and order 
which requires interference by this court. He submits that both the courts 
below not only misread the facts and circumstances but also 
misinterpreted the provisions relates to cause of action as well as 
claiming of suit thus both the courts below committed error by their 
impugned judgment and order. The learned senior counsel placed the 
entire plaint and submits that in the case in hand the plaintiffs have 
challenging a mere power of attorney and such execution of a power of 
attorney by the defendants shall not create any right as emphasized in 
section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned senior counsel placed 
the provisions of Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 
and submits that there is no cause of action at all in the case in hand as 
the said power of attorney is not affecting the right or interest of the 
plaintiff in any manner. The learned senior counsel also drawn the 
attention of this court regarding a prayer wherein the petitioner-plaintiff 
seek a decree upon the court below to appoint certain persons as 
directors which is not permissible in a ordinary suit as the jurisdiction 
lies with other special law. The learned senior counsel further submits 
that this is a fit case for rejection of plaint as because of section 42 of the 
Specific Relief Act as much as the plaint does not disclose any cause of 
action nor the execution of the power of attorney in question shall affect 
the right and character of the plaintiff in any manner. As such, Mr. Arif 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
submits that the instant rule is liable to be made absolute and the plaint 
itself is liable to be rejected on the given facts and circumstances. 
 Mr. Fida M. Kamal, the learned senior counsel appearing on 
behalf of the opposite party vehemently opposes the rule. He submits 
that both the courts below on proper appreciation of the facts and 
circumstances, provisions of law, has rightly rejected the application 
under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 thus the 
courts below committed no error which requires interference by this 
court. He submits that the question of cause of action or other aspects as 
raised by the opposite party-defendants can only be adjudicated at the 
time of trial by framing issues on that point as well as by adducing 
evidence both oral and documentary. He further submits that in the 
present case in hand the petitioner-defendants raises many questions 
which are highly disputed and can only be adjudicated on evidence not 
in limine. The learned senior counsel also placed the provisions of Order 
7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and submits that none of 
the grounds as raised or agitated by the petitioner comes within the 
purview of the aforesaid conditions stipulated thereon and as such the 
courts below committed no illegality in rejecting the application under 
Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The learned 
senior counsel further submits that admittedly in the present case in hand 
the entire assets and the shares have been transferred to the plaintiffs by 
specific agreement which was not only acted upon and the parties are 
about to close the deed and pursuant to the agreement the petitioner 
plaintiffs invested huge sum of money and taking care of the subject 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
matter and such power of attorney under challenged vigorously affecting 
the right and legal character of the plaintiffs and as such at this stage it 
cannot be said that the plaint has nothing to disclose and it is to be 
stopped at the very initiation. The learned senior counsel also placed the 
power of attorney as well as the agreement regarding the transfer of 
shares and other aspects. As such, Mr. Kamal prays for discharging the 
rule for ends of justice. 
I have heard the learned counsels for the petitioners as well as 
opposite parties. I have also perused the impugned judgment and order 
passed by the courts below, revisional application grounds taken thereon, 
application for discharging the rule, provisions of law as well as papers 
and documents filed by both the parties. 
On meticulous perusal of the papers and documents, it transpires 
that the present opposite party as plaintiffs instituted Other Suit No. 367 
of 2020 in the court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chattogram 
impleading the petitioners as defendants for the reliefs as mentioned 
hereinabove. So, it transpires from the aforesaid prayers that apart from 
the prayer for declaring certain persons as directors in prayer-A and B 
the plaintiffs have challenged a registered deed of irrevocable general 
power of attorney duly executed by the defendants. It further transpires 
that after filing of the suit the defendants contested the same by filing 
power. Subsequently, the defendant-petitioner pressed an application 
under Order 7, Rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908. It further transpires that the same was contested in the 
trial court by both the parties and the trial court after hearing the parties 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
and considering the facts and circumstances rejected the same. The 
present petitioner thereafter moved before the learned District Judge, 
Chattogram by way of revision, but the revisional court also affirmed the 
impugned judgment and order passed by the trial court. Order 7, Rule 11 
of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 runs as follows; 
“The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:-- 
(a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action: 
(b) Where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on 
being required by the court to correct the valuation within a 
time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so: 
(c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is 
written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on 
being required by the court to supply the requisite stamp-paper 
within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so: 
(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be 
barred by any law: 
Provided that the time fixed by the court for the correction of 
the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall 
not exceed twenty-one days”. 
So, it transpires that at any stage on an application filed by the 
parties the court preserved the right to reject a plaint. However on 
satisfaction of the provisions as laid down in Order 7, Rule 11 of the 
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Admittedly, in the present case in hand 
both the parties placed several documents and also placed certain issues. 
But the cardinal principle is that in determining whether a plaint is to be 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
rejected, the court will take only the plaint and documents filed thereto 
into consideration and not what has been urged by the defendants in a 
petition or in the written statement. The power to reject a plaint or to 
return it for amendment should not be exercised except in a clear case 
and while dealing with an application under Order 7, Rule 11 of the 
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 it is the duty of the court to apply its 
judicial mind and to see whether the conditions as stipulated in the law 
clearly applicable or not.  
In the present case in hand the main contention of the petitioner is 
that there is no cause of action or the plaintiffs are not entitled to any 
legal right or character to sue. As per the provisions of section 42 of the 
Specific Relief Act a person who also filed a case must entitle to any 
legal right or character as to any property. In the present case in hand on 
meticulous perusal of the plaint, it transpires that a basic claim of the 
plaintiffs rest upon an agreement executed in between the parties on 
28.08.2008 wherein as per the said deed of agreement the entire assets 
and liabilities are to be transferred by the companies in favour of the 
plaintiffs of the suit. The said contract also stipulated the modus 
operandi, process and procedure to be adopted for implementation of the 
said subject matter, namely the companies in question.  
It has been vigorously argued and stated in the plaint that pursuant 
to that agreement the plaintiffs completed major terms and payments and 
about to complete the transaction and at that stage the power of attorney 
has been executed to frustrate the right and character acquired by the 
plaintiffs. On meticulous perusal of the application for rejection of plaint 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
pressed by the parties in the court below it transpires that the defendant-
petitioners admitting the agreement dated 28.08.2008 prayed for 
rejection of the plaint on the ground that the said agreement had become 
void due to the failure of the parties to perform its contractual obligation 
under the aforesaid agreement and after expiry of the same after one year 
there is no subsistent interest giving rights to any cause of action and as 
such the suit must fail at its very inception and there is no necessity to 
dreg a fruitless litigation by harassing the defendant-petitioners. Apart 
from the question of cancellation of the deed the further case as raised by 
the defendant in the application under Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure, 1908 is that instruments for transfer of the shares were 
also void instruments and not permissible in the eye of law furthermore. 
It further transpires from the plaint itself is that the petitioners 
categorically stated that their right as to property and legal character has 
been violated or affected or denied and execution of the said power of 
attorney is a clear denial of the title and right accrued by the plaintiffs by 
virtue of an agreement. So, on meticulous perusal of the papers and 
documents as well as the submissions as advanced by the learned 
counsels it transpires that they raise numerous questions regarding right, 
title, entitlement and subsequent development including cancellation of 
certain agreement etc. It has been mentioned earlier in the light of the 
provision of law, namely Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908 that admittedly if on the averments made in the plaint 
no cause of action is disclosed that the court is bound to reject the plaint 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
and for ascertainment the cause of action the court has to read the plaint 
in its entirety. 
In the present case in hand it transpires that whether the plaintiffs 
at all entitled to any legal character or to any right as to the property 
enabling them to file a suit can only be adjudicated and decided by the 
trial court by framing specific issues and by taking evidence both oral 
and documentary. There is a specific claim pressed by the plaintiffs by 
virtue of an agreement which as per the plaintiffs have already been 
acted upon in majority and as per the plaintiffs the power of attorney 
under challenged is a clear violation and/or affecting the right and 
character of the plaintiffs. On the other hand it has been also vigorously 
challenged by the defendants that the suit is not maintainable as because 
of the expiry of the contract itself and invalidity all the instruments. 
These contentions also required to be examined and adjudicated by the 
trial court by not only framing issues but also by adducing evidence both 
oral and documentary. 
When there is a scope to reject the plaint exercising the power 
under Order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or even 
under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 a heavy duty 
cast upon the court to see whether such provision can be applicable as 
because allowing such application buried the right to sue of a party at the 
very inception and debarred for future litigation. In the present case in 
hand, it transpires that numerous contentions have been raised by both 
the parties which are not only mixed question of facts but also mixed 
question of law and it is now well settled proposition as laid down by 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
this court as well as our apex court that when there is a mixed question 
of facts and law involved as much as vigorous contention has been 
raised such dispute or the real question in controversy can only be 
adjudicated and addressed in a full pledged trial by framing issues and 
taking evidence both oral and documentary. 
Considering the facts and circumstances and provisions of law I 
am of the view that the present case in hand the plaint is not liable to be 
rejected in limine exercising the power conferred under Order 7, Rule 11 
read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 rather can 
only be adjudicated and decided by framing issues and by taking 
evidence both oral and documentary. 
Accordingly, the instant rule is discharged without any order as to 
cost. The impugned judgment and order passed by the courts below are 
hereby affirmed. The trial court is directed to proceed with the suit 
expeditiously, as possible, not later than within 6(six) months from the 
date of receipt of the instant judgment. However, any observation made 
by this court shall not affect the adjudication of the suit by the trial court 
on merit. 
The office is directed to communicate the judgment and order to 
the concerned court below at once. 
 
 
           
 
          
            (Mamnoon Rahman,J:)  
 
 
Emdad. B.O.
input_summary: The plaintiff, a company operating container terminals at Chattogram, sued in 2020 for cancellation of an irrevocable power of attorney registered in 2017 in respect of three companies named in the schedules, for a declaration that three named men were the directors of those companies, and for consequential directions to the sub registrar. Eleven of the defendants applied under Order VII rule 11 for rejection of the plaint as disclosing no cause of action, and the joint district judge threw the application out; the district judge in revision affirmed that order, and the defendants came here.
explanation: The court observed that a power under Order VII rule 11 or section 151 is to be exercised with care, since the rejection of a plaint at the outset buries the plaintiff's right to sue and debars future litigation altogether. It found that the parties had raised numerous contentions about whether the agreement behind the power of attorney had been performed, whether it had expired and whether the instruments were invalid, and that these were mixed questions of fact and law on which the pleadings alone could not yield an answer. Such questions, it held, could only be resolved at a full trial on issues and evidence.

Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Salim 
CIVIL REVISION NO.1045 OF 2009. 
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the deputy 
commissioner, Gopalgonj. 
-------------Defendant No.1-Appellant-Petitioner. 
     -VERSUS- 
Nuruzzaman Mia and others 
                      -------------Opposite Parties. 
Mr. Binoy Kumar Ghosh, A.A.G.

Heard and Judgment on 25.05.2023. 
 
This rule at the instance of the defendant-appellant-petitioner is 
directed against the judgment and decree dated 15.08.2002 passed by the 
Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gopalganj in Title Appeal No.96 of 2001, 
dismissing the appeal in affirming the judgment and decree dated 
16.05.2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Kotalipara, Gopalgonj 
in Title Suit No.36 of 2000 decreeing the suit.  
Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that the opposite party, 
Nos.1 and 2 as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No.36 of 2000 for the 
declaration of title in the suit land and also the declaration that the record 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2 
of the scheduled land in Khas Khatian No.1 in the name of the 
government in the S.A. record prepared wrongly, illegally and not binding 
upon the plaintiffs, and contending that .02 acre of land in plot No.364 of 
R.S. Khatian No.174 under 29 No.  Chhoto Dighalia Mouza belonged to 
Akshay Kumar Saha, who, before R.S. record, used to run a business in a 
shop over the suit land; Akshay Kumar sold the land to Khetra Mohan 
Saha and Monindra Nath Saha by a registered deed No. 768 dated 
5.2.1952.  They continued the business like their vendor.  Subsequently, 
they sold the suit land by a registered Kabala No. 18 dated 2.1.1964 
corresponding to 17 the Poush 1370 BS in favor of Ayub Ali Faraji, a 
resident of Dighalia, and continued the business like his vendor; that 
preliminary S.A. record prepared in the name of Khetra Mohan and 
Monindra, but they did not take any information about final publication 
of the Khatian; that due to enlistment of names in preliminary Khatian, 
they paid rent and obtained Dakhila; that Ayub Ali Faraji, the subsequent 
purchaser did not take information about the S.A. final record at the time 
of his purchase and following in 1966 for 6 point movement Auyb Ali did 
not pay any rent.  After independence, the government remitted the tax 
up to 25 Bighas.  As such, he did not inquire about the S.A. record and, 
while possessing in such position, sold the same by registered kabala No. 
2016 dated 9.8.1984 in favor of the plaintiff.  And used to run the 
business as before that of his vendor; that in the present survey, the suit 
land was recorded in the name of Ayub Ali Fraji; that the suit land in the 
name of East Pakistan Province represented by collector Faridpur was 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3 
recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 which had no basis; that in R.S. Khatian in 
the possession column, the suit land was marked as ‘Chandina’ if so, the 
same not be vested to the government as per law but in S.A. Khatian there 
was no mention of Chandiana in respect of Suit land; that on 27.03.2000 
while plaintiff came to know about the wrong record and received threat 
from the Tahshilder to lease out elsewhere constrained to file the suit.  
Defendant No.1 Government contested the suit by filing a written 
statement denying the plaintiff’s title and possession in the suit land and 
contending inter-alia that the suit land is the Government Khas land as 
Hat-Bazar and accordingly recorded in Khas Khatian No. 1 and finally 
Published and also recorded as the periphery of hat; that the suit land as 
per rule of the government is suitable for lease on a yearly basis and being 
the periferry of Hat and Bhitti, the plaintiff has no right title, interest and 
possession over the same, that the plaintiffs alleged deed No. 768 dated 
5.02.1952, deed No. 2016 dated 2.1.1964 were false and on 27.03.2000 or 
in any dated the Tahshilder did not ask the plaintiff to take the settlement 
of the land as such no cause of action arose.  The suit is liable to be 
dismissed. 
The  Assistant Judge framed as many as six different issues.  The 
plaintiff adduced 5 P.W.s and produced documentary evidence as Exhibit 
1-5, and the defendant side adduced 1 D.W. and documentary evidence as 
Exhibit-‘Ka’.  Subsequently, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 
Kotalipara, Gopalgonj, on the conclusion of the trial by the judgment and 
decree dated 16.05.2001, decreed the suit on the contest. 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the above judgment and 
decree, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No.96 of 2001 before District 
Judge Gopalganj.  On transafer the appeal was heard by the Joint District 
Judge, 1st Court, Gopalganj.  Consequently, The appeal was dismissed by 
the judgment and decree dated 15.08.2002 affirming those passed by the 
Assistant Judge. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree, 
the defendant-appellant-petitioner preferred the revision application 
before this court and obtained the instant rule.  
 
Mr. Mr. Binoy Kumar Ghosh, the learned Assistant Attorney 
General appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that admittedly, 
the suit land is a government periphery and recorded as Khas Khatian 
No.1 as Hat; the appellate court as well as trial court belo without 
discussing any evidence on record held title possession in favor of the 
plaintiff and decreed the suit; the suit is barred as per the provision under 
sub-rule 2a of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 
On the other hand, Ms. Purabi Saha, learned counsel appearing on 
behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that both the court below 
concurrently found that the plaintiffs have succeeded in proving their case 
and in the impugned judgment and decree there is no misreading or non-
reading evidence of record.   The plaintiffs have been able to prove their 
title and possession in the suit land, and both the courts below have not 
committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision 
occasioning a failure of justice. 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5 
I have heard the learned counsel for both parties and considered 
their submissions.   I have perused the judgment and decree passed by 
both the courts below, as well as evidence of witnesses and other material 
evidence on record.  
The onus lies upon the plaintiffs to prove their settlement, title, and 
possession in the suit land.   To prove their settlement, title, and 
possession, the plaintiffs have examined four(4) witnesses.  Of them, 
P.W.1 Nazmul Islam admitted in the cross-examination that he has a shop 
in the suit land; after the burning of the shop they did not see Ayub Ali 
Faraji as the shopkeeper of the Bazar. He denied the suggestion that the 
suit land belongs to the periferry of Hat or deeds are void, febricated and 
created. P.W.2 Ayob Ali Farazi admitted in the cross-examination that 
suit land belongs to the Hat; this land belongs to the Chandina Vita. 
P.W.3 Badsha Mia admitted in the cross-examination that suit land is the 
shop house; the plaintiff’s shop is Chandina Vita.  P.W.4 Md. Yakub Ali 
Khan admitted in the chief that he is a businessman of the market. In 
cross-examination he also admitted that suit land belongs to the 
government khash khatian No.1. Moreover, the plaintiffs failed to exhibit 
any kind of rent receipts or  Dakhila to prove their respective possession 
in the suit land.   
Further, from exhibit-1, the C.S. record manifests that the 
classification of the suit land is Chandina; exabit-2  that the S.A. record of 
the suit land has been recorded as Khas Khatian No.1, i.e., the  periferry of 
the hat and Exihibit-2ka the R.S record of the suit land has also been 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6 
recorded as Khas Khatian No.1. On the other hand,  D.W.1 deposed that 
the R.S. record of the land in question remained in the name of the East 
Pakistan Province represented by the collector, Faridpur, in Khas Khatian 
No.1 and finally published as the periferry of hat; chandina means the 
land belongs to Hat-Bazar.  Nevertheless, it is admitted that the suit land 
belongs to the Khas Khatian No.1, i.e., the periphery of the hat.   
In view of the above , I am of the view that plaintiffs have failed to 
prove their land settlement and have failed to prove their title and 
possession of the suit land and the plaintiffs’ case is barred by law as per 
the provision so enumerated in sub-section (2a) of section 20 of the State 
Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950.   This view gets support from the case 
of the Province of East Pakistan Vs Md.  Shahabuddin Gazi and others 
reported in 25 DLR(AD) 248 held that— 
 After the retrospective amendment made by Ordinance No. XII of 
1960 in section 20 of the Act by the incorporation therein of sub-section 
(2a), which had the effect of excluding hats and bazars from the category 
of returnable lands from the very beginning, the hats and bazars in the 
khas possession of the rent-receiver became vested in the government 
from the date of the notification in 1956 under sub-section 2 of section 3 
of the Act.  But so far as raiyats, agricultural tenants, and other tenants 
were concerned, the vesting took place after the preparation and final 
publication of the compensation assessment roll and its notification by 
virtue of subsection (3) of section 44 of the Act.   

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7 
A similar view has been taken in 9 DLR(HCD) 569.  On the above 
facts, circumstances of the case, and discussions made herein above, I am 
of the firm view that the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gopalganj, 
did not correctly appreciate and construe the documents and materials on 
record in accordance with the law in affirming the judgment and decree of 
the trial court.  Therefore, the impugned judgment and decree dated 
15.08.2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, 
Gopalganj, in affirming the judgment and decree dated 16.05.2001 passed 
by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kotalipara, Gopalgonj suffers from 
legal infirmity and perversity, and as such, the same is liable to be set 
aside. 
As a result, the rule is made absolutely without any order regarding 
costs.  
The judgment and decree dated 15.08.2002 passed by the learned 
Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gopalganj, in Title Appeal No.96 of 2001 
dismissing the appeal in affirming the judgment and decree dated 
16.05.2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kotalipara, 
Gopalgonj in Title Suit No.36 of 2000 is hereby set aside. 
 
Let the Lower Court Records be sent down with required copies of 
the judgment at once.

input_summary: Two plaintiffs sued in 2000 for a declaration of title over two decimals of land at Kotalipara in Gopalganj and for a declaration that the entry of the land in the government's khas khatian as part of a market was wrong, tracing their title through sales of 1952, 1964 and 1984 and pleading that they had been running a shop on the land throughout. The trial court decreed the suit and the joint district judge in appeal affirmed that decree, so the government came here in revision, contending that the land was the periphery of a hat and had vested in it long ago.
